evidence: All referenced figures are correct: Ch 5's 50 tok/s (20 ms/token) is [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]; canonical batch-1 is 40 tok/s (25 ms/token); Ch 15's ~8.5K tok/s is prefill-side; ~35,000–56,000 tok/s is batched serving. The parenthetical correctly prevents the reader from mistaking 50 tok/s for the host's aggregate rate.

page_hint: Ch 5, §2, 'Mental Model' — the input-heavy vs output-heavy paragraph
quoted_clause: If the workload is input-heavy (9.2K average input, 300-token output, ~30× more input than output), the system is first-order memory-capacity-bound (KV residency at the Ch 17 concurrency screen) and prefill-dominated in FLOPs — a first-order tendency to verify per workload, not a consequence of input-heaviness alone. If the workload were output-heavy, the token/FLOP mix shifts toward decode, which often makes decode bandwidth or latency critical — the actual bottleneck must be measured on the target stack.
observed: The paragraph correctly hedges both claims ('first-order tendency to verify per workload,' 'the actual bottleneck must be measured'). However, the phrase 'memory-capacity-bound' is used without the full three-bound distinction that Ch 8 §1 establishes (compute-bound vs memory-bandwidth-bound vs memory-capacity-constrained). A reader encountering this in Ch 5 (before Ch 8) may conflate 'memory-capacity-bound' with 'memory-bandwidth-bound.' The Ch 8 distinction is the correct one, but Ch 5 uses the term before it is defined.
evidence: Ch 8 §1: 'Three different bounds — keep them apart. Compute-bound means... Memory-bandwidth-bound (what the roofline calls memory-bound) means... Memory-capacity-constrained (often KV-capacity-constrained in long-context inference) means feasible concurrency or context is limited by how much data fits in HBM.' Ch 5's 'memory-capacity-bound' matches the third definition but the reader has not yet seen the distinction.
root_cause: Ch 5 uses a term that is precisely defined in Ch 8, creating a forward-dependency on a distinction the reader has not yet learned.
correction: Either (a) add a brief inline definition: 'first-order memory-capacity-bound (the KV cache's HBM footprint limits how many concurrent requests fit — distinct from memory-bandwidth-bound, where the rate of HBM reads limits per-token speed; Ch 8 §1 formalizes the three-way distinction)'; or (b) rephrase to avoid the term: 'first-order limited by KV-cache HBM capacity (the per-request KV footprint constrains concurrency at the Ch 17 screen) and prefill-dominated in FLOPs.' Option (b) is simpler and avoids the forward reference.
acceptance_test: A reader who has not yet read Ch 8 can distinguish the 'memory-capacity' constraint (how many requests fit) from a 'memory-bandwidth' constraint (how fast each token is produced) based on Ch 5's text alone.

page_hint: Ch 7, §1, 'Count state by lifetime, not by the model label' — the 256-position canvas example
quoted_clause: As a shape-only example, a 256-position canvas over a 262,144-entry vocabulary needs 256 × 262,144 × 4 = 268,435,456 bytes, or 256 MiB, for one FP32 logits tensor at batch one. This excludes probabilities, sampling workspace, retained logits, attention buffers and the rest of the model. It is not a measured model footprint.
observed: The calculation is correct (256 × 262,144 × 4 = 268,435,456 = 256 MiB). However, the example's purpose (illustrating that a diffusion runtime's peak memory is not captured by the AR weights+KV formula) is not made explicit before the number. The reader must infer why a 256 MiB logits tensor is relevant to the 'count state by lifetime' principle. The sentence 'This excludes probabilities, sampling workspace, retained logits, attention buffers and the rest of the model' is a list of exclusions that does not help the reader understand what the 256 MiB figure is *for*.
evidence: 256 × 262,144 = 67,108,864; × 4 = 268,435,456 B = 256 MiB. ✓. The point is that a single intermediate tensor (logits for 256 positions) can be 256 MiB, which is non-trivial relative to a 24 GB device's budget, and that this tensor is not part of the AR KV cache formula.
root_cause: The example was written as a shape calculation without a preceding sentence stating the architectural point it illustrates.
correction: Prepend one sentence: 'A diffusion runtime's peak memory includes intermediate tensors (logits, attention scores, sampling buffers) that have no analogue in the AR weights+KV formula. For example, a 256-position canvas over a 262,144-entry vocabulary produces a single FP32 logits tensor of 256 × 262,144 × 4 = 256 MiB at batch one — a non-trivial fraction of a 24 GB device's budget, and a cost the AR formula does not capture. This excludes the remaining model state (probabilities, sampling workspace, retained logits, attention buffers, weights).'
acceptance_test: A reader can state in one sentence why the 256 MiB figure matters for the 'count state by lifetime' principle, without re-reading the paragraph.

page_hint: Ch 8, §3, 'Prefill PFLOP for 9.2K input' — the initial 1.29 PFLOP figure
quoted_clause: the prefill FLOP cost is: 2 × N × L = 2 × 70 × 10^9 × 9.2 × 10^3 ≈ 1.29 PFLOP [DERIVED: 2 × N × L where N=70B, L=9,200; the figure is large because the full context is attended to, but it is a one-time cost per request, not a sustained rate]
observed: The 1.29 PFLOP figure is presented as 'the prefill FLOP cost' before the three-case accounting (linear-only, full-square, causal-triangle) is introduced two paragraphs later. The [DERIVED] note says 'the figure is large because the full context is attended to' which is slightly misleading: the 2NL figure is large because it multiplies by L, but the 'full context is attended to' phrase suggests the attention term is included, when it is not. The reader may carry the 1.29 as the 'true' prefill cost until the three-case section corrects it.
evidence: The 2NL = 1.288 PFLOP is the linear-only (case i) figure. The full-square (case ii) is 1.5099 PFLOP (+17.23%). The causal (case iii) is 1.3989 PFLOP (+8.61%). The [DERIVED] note's phrase 'the figure is large because the full context is attended to' conflates the linear scaling with L (which is correct) with the attention mechanism (which is the quadratic term, not included in 2NL).
root_cause: The initial figure was written as a simple 2NL calculation with a brief note, before the three-case section was added. The note's language was not updated to reflect that the attention term is excluded.
correction: Change the [DERIVED] note to: '[DERIVED: 2 × N × L where N=70B, L=9,200; this is the linear (projection) term only — the quadratic attention term adds ~17% at 9.2K (case (ii), below). The figure is a one-time cost per request, not a sustained rate.]' This prevents the reader from treating 1.29 as the complete prefill cost.
acceptance_test: A reader who stops after the 1.29 PFLOP figure and its [DERIVED] note understands that the attention term is not included, without needing to read the three-case section.

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(b), 'Economics unit note (reconciliation with Ch. 4 and Ch. 15)'
quoted_clause: Both chapters use the same on-demand price basis: ~$2.50/hr per H100 → ~$20/hr per 8×H100 host. Two things must be kept straight. First, units: both chapters express tokens per dollar — this chapter computes it as token-rate × 3600 s ÷ hourly cost (50 × 3600 ÷ 20 = 9,000 tokens per dollar), which is algebraically identical to token-rate ÷ per-second cost (50 ÷ (20/3600) = 9,000); no 3600 factor separates the two formulas.
observed: The reconciliation note is correct and addresses a real potential confusion (the 3600 factor). However, it is 120 words long and appears in the middle of the worked example's economics section, interrupting the flow from the 9,000 tokens/$ calculation to the prefill+decode combined calculation. The note's purpose is to prevent a specific misreading (that Ch 4 and Ch 15 use a different formula), but its length and placement make it feel like a digression rather than a clarification.
evidence: 50 × 3600 / 20 = 9,000. 50 / (20/3600) = 50 / 0.00556 = 9,000. The two formulas are algebraically identical. The note correctly identifies that the ~50 tok/s here is a low-batch decode rate, distinct from Ch 15's prefill-side ~8.5K tok/s and batched serving ~35,000–56,000 tok/s.
root_cause: The reconciliation was written as a full paragraph to be self-contained, but in context it functions as a scope note that could be more compact.
correction: Compress to 3–4 sentences: 'Scope: the ~50 tok/s is this example's low-batch decode rate (20 ms/token), not the host's batched serving throughput (Ch 15: ~35,000–56,000 tok/s) or its prefill-side rate (~8.5K tok/s). The 9,000 tokens/$ is a floor set by the single-stream assumption. Ch 4 and Ch 15 use the same $20/hr price basis; the token-rate inputs differ by phase and batch, not by formula.' Move the algebraic identity note (50×3600/20 = 50/(20/3600)) to a footnote or omit it (it is trivially verifiable).
acceptance_test: The economics section flows from the 9,000 tokens/$ calculation to the prefill+decode combined calculation without a 120-word interruption, and the scope distinction is still clearly stated.

page_hint: Ch 10, §1 Concept, data parallelism framing

observed: For plain DP the gradient-sync point is the main communication event, but FSDP also all-gathers parameter shards before computation and reduce-scatters gradients afterward. The sentence can be read as saying FSDP's communication load is only at gradient sync, contradicting the later FSDP paragraph.

correction: Split the claim: 'For plain DP, the communication load is at the gradient-sync point; FSDP also communicates during the forward pass when it all-gathers parameter shards, and during backward when it reduce-scatters gradients.'

page_hint: Ch 16 §16.3, Mode 1, 'Per request' paragraph; also Ch 16 §16.3 'Feasible served-volume bound' paragraph
quoted_clause: 10 rps × 8 h × 3,600 s × 260 workdays ÷ 12 = 6,240,000 requests/month, not 24×7; request-active time is 173.33 h/month
observed: The formula is arithmetically correct (74,880,000/12 = 6,240,000) but the '÷ 12' is unexplained. A reader sees '260 workdays' (an annual figure) multiplied by '8 h' (a daily figure) and then divided by 12 without being told that 260 is per-year and ÷12 converts to per-month. The resulting '173.33 h/month' active time (≈ 21.7 business days × 8 h) is consistent, but the formula as written looks like an arbitrary adjustment.
evidence: 260 workdays/year ÷ 12 months/year = 21.67 workdays/month. 21.67 × 8 h × 3,600 s/h = 624,096 s ≈ 624,000 s. 10 rps × 624,000 s = 6,240,000 req/mo. The '÷ 12' is the year-to-month conversion.
root_cause: The formula compresses two steps (annual-to-monthly conversion, then rate × time) into one line without labeling the '÷ 12' as a unit conversion.
correction: Rewrite as: '10 rps × 8 h/day × 3,600 s/h × (260 workdays/yr ÷ 12 mo/yr) = 10 × 8 × 3,600 × 21.67 ≈ 6,240,000 requests/month (active business-hours window; 173.33 h/mo of 8-h days, not 24×7).' Or simply: '10 rps × 173.33 h/mo × 3,600 s/h = 6,240,000 requests/month, where 173.33 h = 8 h × 21.67 business days (260/12).'
acceptance_test: A reader who does not know the canonical workload should be able to follow the derivation of 6,240,000 from the stated inputs without guessing what '÷ 12' represents.
